source_user: Define decode and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Definition. Decode is the autoregressive phase of LLM inference: after the prompt is processed (prefill), the model emits one token per forward step, each step attending over the growing KV cache. Batch-token count per step is ~B (one token per sequence), versus ~B*S in prefill.

Why it matters. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, not FLOP bound. Concrete mechanism: at batch size B and dtype fp16, each step must stream the full weight set (e.g. ~18 GB for a 9B model in bf16) from HBM plus read the per-sequence KV cache; arithmetic intensity is ~O(B) FLOPs per byte, so with small B the GEMMs degenerate into GEMV and the SM array idles waiting on HBM. Upper bound on step latency: t_step >= (W_bytes + KV_bytes) / BW_HBM. On an A30 (933 GB/s), an 18 GB weight read alone floors t_step at ~19 ms, i.e. ~52 tok/s per sequence regardless of compute.

Boundary condition. This bandwidth-bound regime holds only while B is small enough that weight streaming dominates. As B grows, weight bytes amortize across sequences and KV traffic (which scales linearly with B*context) takes over; past some B* the kernel becomes compute- or KV-bandwidth-bound and per-token latency rises again. Long contexts move B* down because KV bytes per step grow with sequence length.

Falsifiable claim: if decode is weight-bandwidth bound, doubling B should increase throughput near-linearly while leaving per-step latency nearly flat.

Evidence to collect: measured tokens/s vs batch size curve, DCGM/Nsight HBM read bytes per step, achieved occupancy, and KV cache bytes per step.

Rollback gate: if a scheduling or batching change raises p99 TTFT or inter-token latency beyond the SLO on a canary at <=5% traffic, revert.

source_user: Define decode and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Definition. Decode is the token-by-token generation phase of LLM inference following prefill. Each step performs a forward pass over exactly one new token per sequence, reading all model weights and the accumulated KV cache, then appending one KV entry per layer.

Why it matters. It dominates end-to-end latency for long outputs and it is the phase whose cost model differs most from training. Concrete mechanism: the per-step attention reads KV of size 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * dtype_bytes per sequence. For a 9B-class model with GQA (say 8 KV heads, 128 head_dim, 40 layers, bf16), that is ~160 KB per token per sequence, so a 32k-context sequence carries ~5 GB of KV. At batch 16 the KV alone exceeds the free HBM on a 24 GB A30 after weights, forcing eviction, recompute, or offload.

Boundary condition. The KV-dominant regime applies when B * seq_len * per_token_KV exceeds the weight footprint; below that threshold weight streaming dominates and KV pressure is irrelevant. Paged attention / block allocation changes fragmentation, not the total bytes.

Falsifiable claim: if KV bytes dominate, per-step latency should grow roughly linearly in mean context length at fixed batch size.

Evidence to collect: KV bytes allocated per step, HBM read volume, preemption/swap counts from the serving engine, and latency vs context-length sweep.

Rollback gate: revert any KV or quantization change if canary shows accuracy regression on a held-out generative eval or if preemption rate exceeds the pre-change baseline.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Contrast. The naive implementation is decode without a KV cache: to produce token t it re-runs full self-attention over all t-1 previous tokens every step. Real decode caches per-layer K and V and only computes the query for the new token.

Concrete mechanism. Naive recompute costs O(t) attention work per step, so generating N tokens is O(N^2) total attention FLOPs and O(N^2) weight-independent activation traffic. Cached decode costs O(t) memory reads but O(1) attention compute for the new query, so generating N tokens is O(N) forward passes with O(N^2) cumulative KV reads but no recomputation of past projections. Empirically this converts a compute-bound quadratic into a bandwidth-bound linear-per-step loop; the crossover is immediate, naive is never faster beyond a handful of tokens.

Boundary condition. The cache trades compute for memory: KV bytes = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * dtype_bytes per sequence. When aggregate KV would exceed free HBM, the naive recompute path (or partial recompute / chunked prefill of evicted blocks) becomes the only feasible option, so the cached path is strictly better only inside the memory envelope.

Falsifiable claim: with cache enabled, per-step latency should be near-flat in output position; without it, per-step latency should rise linearly.

Evidence to collect: per-step latency vs token index for both paths, HBM occupancy, and eviction/recompute counters.

Rollback gate: if enabling recompute-on-evict raises p99 inter-token latency past SLO on a 5% canary, revert to smaller max batch instead.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Contrast. Naive decode implementations run one sequence at a time with static batching: the batch is formed once, and every sequence in it must finish before the next batch starts. Production decode uses continuous (in-flight) batching, where finished sequences are evicted and new ones admitted at each step.

Concrete mechanism. In static batching the batch's step count equals the longest generation in it, so GPU slots occupied by already-finished short sequences do nothing; utilization is mean_len/max_len. With a mixed distribution where mean output is 100 tokens and max is 2000, static batching wastes ~95% of the slot-steps at the tail. Continuous batching re-packs the running set each iteration, keeping the token budget near the configured maximum and raising achieved throughput several-fold at the same hardware.

Boundary condition. Continuous batching only helps when arrival rate is high enough to keep a queue; under light load there is nothing to backfill with, and its extra scheduling overhead plus preemption logic can slightly raise per-step latency. It also requires paged/blocked KV allocation, otherwise fragmentation prevents admitting new sequences.

Falsifiable claim: throughput gain from continuous batching should vanish as offered load drops below the point where the queue empties.

Evidence to collect: running-batch-size histogram per step, queue depth, throughput and p99 latency vs offered QPS for both schedulers.

Rollback gate: revert if p99 TTFT regresses beyond SLO or preemption rate exceeds an agreed ceiling on a canary.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Contrast. A naive implementation co-locates prefill and decode in the same batch on the same GPU with no scheduling separation. Disaggregated or chunked designs separate them, because the two phases have opposite bottlenecks.

Concrete mechanism. Prefill is compute-bound: it processes S tokens at once, so its GEMMs have high arithmetic intensity and saturate tensor cores. Decode is bandwidth-bound with ~1 token per sequence. When a long prefill (say 8k tokens) is interleaved into a decode batch, every running decode sequence stalls for the full prefill duration, producing an inter-token-latency spike of tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Chunked prefill splits the prompt into fixed token-budget slices (e.g. 512 tokens) so each iteration mixes a bounded prefill chunk with decode work; prefill/decode disaggregation goes further, running the phases on separate GPU pools and shipping the KV cache over the interconnect (this is the model Mooncake and NVIDIA Dynamo style architectures adopt).

Boundary condition. Disaggregation only pays off when KV transfer cost is small relative to the recompute it avoids; that needs high-bandwidth links (NVLink or RDMA/RoCE with GPUDirect). On a commodity TCP fabric the transfer can exceed the prefill it saved.

Falsifiable claim: chunked prefill should flatten the inter-token-latency tail without materially lowering aggregate throughput.

Evidence to collect: ITL distribution with and without chunking, prefill chunk budget sweep, and measured KV transfer bytes/time if disaggregating.

Rollback gate: revert if TTFT rises beyond SLO or if KV transfer time exceeds the measured prefill time it replaced.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Contrast. A naive decode loop uses greedy or single-token stepping with no speculation. Speculative decoding instead runs a cheap draft model (or n-gram / Medusa head) to propose k tokens, then verifies them in one target-model forward pass.

Concrete mechanism. Because decode is bandwidth-bound, a forward pass over k proposed tokens costs almost the same wall time as a pass over 1 token: the dominant term is streaming the weights once. Verification accepts the longest prefix consistent with the target distribution, so expected tokens per target pass is 1 + sum of acceptance probabilities. With acceptance rate alpha and draft length k, expected accepted length is (1 - alpha^(k+1))/(1 - alpha); at alpha=0.7, k=4 this is ~2.8 tokens per target pass, a ~2.8x latency reduction minus draft cost. Rejection sampling in the verifier makes the output distribution identical to plain decode, so quality is unchanged by construction.

Boundary condition. The win collapses when the batch is already large: at high B the target pass is no longer weight-bandwidth bound, so processing k*B tokens costs proportionally more and speculation adds work without saving time. It also collapses when alpha is low (domain mismatch between draft and target).

Falsifiable claim: measured speedup should track (accepted tokens per target pass) / (1 + draft overhead) and should decay toward 1.0 as batch size grows.

Evidence to collect: acceptance rate histogram, tokens per target pass, end-to-end tok/s vs batch size, and a distribution-equivalence check against non-speculative output.

Rollback gate: disable speculation if measured speedup < 1.1x at production batch sizes or if any output-distribution equivalence test fails.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Contrast. A naive implementation allocates a contiguous, max-length KV buffer per sequence. Paged attention allocates KV in fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) from a shared pool with a per-sequence block table.

Concrete mechanism. Contiguous preallocation must reserve max_seq_len regardless of actual output length, so a request that generates 100 tokens under a 32k limit wastes 99.7% of its reservation; internal fragmentation caps concurrency far below what HBM could support. Paged allocation reserves only blocks actually used, bounding waste to at most one partial block per sequence (<= block_size - 1 tokens), which lifts achievable running batch size by a large factor on the same GPU. It also makes prefix sharing possible: identical system prompts map to the same physical blocks with refcounts, so copy-on-write avoids duplicating shared prefixes.

Boundary condition. The gain is proportional to the variance in output length and to the ratio max_seq_len/mean_seq_len. If every request generates near the max length, paging saves almost nothing and its block-table indirection adds a small per-step gather cost. Very small block sizes increase metadata and kernel overhead.

Falsifiable claim: achievable concurrent sequences under paging should approach total_KV_HBM / (mean_context * per_token_KV), versus total_KV_HBM / (max_context * per_token_KV) without it.

Evidence to collect: block pool utilization, running batch size, fragmentation ratio, prefix cache hit rate, and per-step attention kernel time with and without paging.

Rollback gate: revert a block-size change if attention kernel time regresses more than an agreed percentage or if OOM/preemption events appear on canary.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes / trade-offs of decode.

1) KV cache exhaustion under load. Mechanism: KV bytes per sequence = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * context_len * dtype_bytes and grow every step. As concurrency and context rise, the KV pool saturates; the engine then preempts or swaps sequences, and preempted sequences must recompute their prefill on resume. This produces a bimodal latency distribution and, in the worst case, a livelock where the system spends most of its time recomputing evicted prefixes rather than generating. Boundary condition: this only occurs above the concurrency where B * mean_context * per_token_KV exceeds free HBM after weights and activation workspace.

2) Latency/throughput trade-off from batching. Mechanism: because decode streams weights once per step regardless of B, raising B raises throughput near-linearly while per-step latency stays roughly flat, until KV reads and GEMM compute dominate; past that point inter-token latency climbs and queueing delay compounds it. Boundary condition: the flat region ends at the B where KV bytes per step approach weight bytes per step; long contexts collapse that region toward B=1.

Falsifiable claims: (a) preemption counters should be zero below the computed KV concurrency limit and rise sharply above it; (b) the tok/s vs B curve should show a knee at the predicted B*.

Evidence to collect: KV pool utilization time series, preemption/recompute counts, tok/s and p99 ITL vs batch size sweep, HBM read bytes per step.

Rollback gate: cap max running sequences at the empirically measured knee minus a margin; roll back any increase that produces nonzero preemptions or p99 ITL above SLO on a 5% canary.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes / trade-offs of decode.

1) Head-of-line blocking from long prefills. Mechanism: a scheduler that admits a full-length prefill into the decode loop makes every running sequence wait for that compute-bound pass, so inter-token latency spikes by the prefill duration (an 8k-token prefill can be tens to hundreds of ms). Chunked prefill with a fixed token budget per iteration bounds the spike, at the cost of slightly higher TTFT for the prefilling request. Boundary condition: only material when prompt lengths are heavy-tailed; with uniformly short prompts the spike is below the SLO and chunking is pure overhead.

2) Quantization of KV or weights trading accuracy for capacity. Mechanism: dropping KV from fp16 to fp8/int8 halves or quarters KV bytes, directly raising the concurrency ceiling and lowering per-step KV read time, but introduces quantization error that compounds autoregressively across generation steps, so degradation is worse for long outputs than short ones. Boundary condition: acceptable only where a generative eval on the target domain shows no regression beyond an agreed threshold at the maximum supported output length; per-token perplexity on short sequences is not a sufficient check.

Falsifiable claims: (a) ITL tail should shrink monotonically as the prefill chunk budget decreases; (b) quantized-KV quality gap should widen with output length if the compounding hypothesis holds.

Evidence to collect: ITL percentiles vs chunk budget, TTFT distribution, generative eval scores stratified by output length for each KV dtype, KV pool utilization.

Rollback gate: revert quantization if any stratified eval bucket regresses beyond the agreed threshold; revert chunking if TTFT p99 exceeds SLO.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes / trade-offs of decode.

1) Tensor-parallel communication overhead dominating at low batch. Mechanism: decode with TP=N inserts two all-reduces per transformer layer on activations of size B * hidden * dtype_bytes. At B=1 these messages are tiny (kilobytes), so the all-reduce is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound, and NCCL launch plus link latency per layer can rival the GEMM time it parallelizes. Scaling TP from 2 to 8 can therefore reduce per-token latency sublinearly or even worsen it once the interconnect is PCIe rather than NVLink. Boundary condition: TP scaling pays off for decode only when the per-GPU weight shard read time still dominates the per-layer collective latency; that holds at larger models, larger batches, and high-bandwidth low-latency links.

2) Stragglers and tail amplification in multi-GPU / multi-node decode. Mechanism: every decode step is a synchronization barrier across all TP ranks, so step latency equals the slowest rank. A single GPU with thermal throttling, an ECC-retired page, or a degraded NIC lane raises p99 for the whole replica, not just itself. Boundary condition: this only manifests as user-visible tail latency when the straggler's excess exceeds the scheduler's slack; brief jitter is absorbed.

Falsifiable claims: (a) per-token latency vs TP degree should flatten or invert below a predictable batch size; (b) removing the suspected straggler rank should restore p99 to the fleet baseline.

Evidence to collect: NCCL collective timings per layer (NCCL_DEBUG / profiler), per-rank step time distribution, link type and measured bus bandwidth, DCGM clock-throttle and ECC counters.

Rollback gate: revert a TP-degree increase if measured p50/p99 per-token latency does not improve at production batch size; drain any rank whose step time exceeds the fleet median by an agreed margin.
